Everything you need is from this morning's sessions. When you're stuck, check `?function_name`, the [ggplot2 reference](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/), and any other R documentation *ONLY* -- no AI tools for this task, please. (It's for your own good.)

## Setup (given) {.unnumbered}

Run this as is — it loads the packages and builds the `counties` data frame from this morning:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)

counties <- left_join(
  read_csv("https://princeton-ddss.github.io/r-bootcamp/files/county_data.csv"),
  read_csv("https://princeton-ddss.github.io/r-bootcamp/files/county_population.csv"),
  join_by(GEOID == fips)
)
```
:::


# Part 1: the county data

## A histogram, dressed up

Draw a histogram of county median **rent** with `geom_histogram()`:

- pick a `bins` value that shows the shape
- add real axis labels and a title with `labs()`


::: {.cell}

:::


*Your answer:* Describe the shape of the distribution in one or two sentences. Where is the bulk of counties? Is there a tail?

## Layer by layer

Build up a scatterplot of **rent (y) against income (x)** from layers:

1.  All counties in gray (`geom_point()` with `color = "gray"` and a small `size`)
2.  The counties of one state you care about on top, in color — hint: a geom can bring its own data, e.g. `geom_point(data = filter(counties, state == "..."), ...)`
3.  A horizontal reference line at the national median rent (`geom_hline()`)
4.  Proper labels with `labs()`


::: {.cell}

:::


*Your answer:* Where does your state sit relative to the national pattern?

## Set vs. map

In the last task you *set* colors by hand — and got no legend. Now *map* **region to color** inside `aes()`, then swap the mapping to **division** and look again.


::: {.cell}

:::


*Your answer:* What appeared automatically that you never built in the previous task? And does color still work well with nine divisions?

## Distributions by group

Show the distribution of **rent by region** using `geom_boxplot()`. Add proper labels with `labs()`.


::: {.cell}

:::


*Your answer:* Which region has the highest median rent? The widest spread?

## Composition

Create a `rent_level` column splitting counties at the median **rent** — `mutate()` with `if_else()`, like this morning. Then make a stacked bar chart of **region filled by `rent_level`** — first as counts, then with `position = "fill"`.


::: {.cell}

:::


*Your answer:* Which version answers "which region has the most high-rent counties?" and which answers "which region is most dominated by them?"

## Small multiples

Facet the income–rent scatterplot by **division** — finer than region, so nine panels — and put income on a **log scale**.


::: {.cell}

:::


*Your answer:* Does the income–rent relationship look similar across divisions? Which divisions sit highest?

## Publication-ready

Take your favorite plot from above and make it something you'd put in a paper or presentation:

- a complete theme with a `base_size` chosen for your medium
- a deliberate color palette (`scale_*_viridis_*`, `scale_*_brewer()`, or `scale_*_manual()`)
- complete labels, including title and legend title

Then save it with `ggsave()` **as a PDF**.


::: {.cell}

:::


*Your answer:* Why did we save a PDF instead of taking a screenshot?

# Part 2 (stretch): mapping America's partisan shift

A real-world finale — no more prepared course files. You'll fetch county-level presidential returns from the MIT Election Data + Science Lab, wrangle them, explore them flat, and finish with a county map of the 2012 → 2024 shift in the Republican vote share. If you don't get here before lunch, it makes a great take-home.

## Go get the data

Real analyses start at someone else's download page:

1.  Go to the MIT Election Lab's [County Presidential Election Returns 2000–2024](https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/VOQCHQ) on the Harvard Dataverse.
2.  Download `countypres_2000-2024.tab`, and in the download menu **choose "Comma Separated Values (Original File Format)"** — the default hands you a tab-delimited conversion with a misleading name.
3.  Save it next to this `.qmd`, then load it with `read_csv()` and inspect it (`glimpse()`, `count(pres, year)`, a few rows).


::: {.cell}

:::


*Your answer:* What does one row of this data represent? And look closely at `county_fips` in your `glimpse()` output — what did `read_csv()` do to it that should worry you? (Friday's FIPS lesson…)

## Republican vote share, by county and year

Build a table with one row per county per year, for **2012 and 2024** only, holding the Republican share of the vote. A recipe:

- `filter()` to the two years, and drop rows with a missing `county_fips`
- also drop the bookkeeping rows a few states include in 2024 (`TOTAL VOTES CAST`, `OVERVOTES`, …) — they have an empty `party`, so `filter(party != "")` does it. Skip this and your denominator double-counts!
- rebuild proper five-character GEOIDs: `str_pad(county_fips, width = 5, pad = "0")`
- `group_by()` year and GEOID, then `summarize()` with `rep_share = sum(candidatevotes[party == "REPUBLICAN"]) / sum(candidatevotes)`

That last line is Friday's subset-by-condition working inside `summarize()`. Summing over *all* remaining rows also quietly handles another quirk: some states report votes by mode (election day, early, absentee, …) rather than one total — extra rows per county, but a share doesn't care.


::: {.cell}

:::


*Your answer:* Sanity-check yourself: roughly how many rows should this table have, and does it?

## Explore flat before you map

Maps are seductive; look at the distributions first.

- Reshape to one row per county with `pivot_wider()` — `pivot_longer()`'s mirror image (`names_from = year, values_from = rep_share, names_prefix = "y"`) — and compute `shift = y2024 - y2012`
- Plot 2024 share against 2012 share and add `geom_abline()` — the 45° line where nothing changed
- Plot a histogram of `shift`


::: {.cell}

:::


*Your answer:* What does a county above the 45° line mean? Where does the bulk of counties sit relative to it?

## The map

Load the county boundaries (as in this morning's session):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(sf)
shapes <- st_read(
  "https://princeton-ddss.github.io/r-bootcamp/files/county_shapes.geojson"
)
```
:::


Then map the shift:

- `left_join()` your shift table onto `shapes` by GEOID (joins work on sf objects too)
- `geom_sf(aes(fill = shift))`
- Use a diverging fill so the map reads like the politics: `scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", mid = "white", high = "red")` — blue where the Republican share *fell*, red where it *rose*
- `theme_void()`


::: {.cell}

:::


*Your answer:* Which regions moved hardest toward the Republicans, and where did the shift run the other way? Some counties also come out gray (no data) — which states, and why might that be? (Think back to yesterday's Connecticut join mismatch.)

*Election data: MIT Election Data and Science Lab, "County Presidential Election Returns 2000–2024", [doi:10.7910/DVN/VOQCHQ](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/VOQCHQ) (CC0).*
